doc.title: Ruth & Bucky Pizzarelli interviewed by Monk Rowe, Saddle River, New Jersey, January 19, 2015

title: The end of the studio years and playing live again
summary: Bucky dates his studio years from the late 50s to early 70s; calls dried up, he went back to live playing, and recalls Kate Smith and the Three Suns.

story.theme_name: Jazz musicians in the movies and film scoring
story.community_name: Studio work and jingles: New York session life

blocks.x: So you’re saying during the “glory years” of the studio, what years did that encompass?
Oh I would say from late 50s, all of the 60s, into the 70s, like ‘70, ‘71, ’72.
Did you decide to get out of it or did it just sort of —
It dried up. And why did it dry up?
I don’t know why. Because all of a sudden there weren’t any calls coming in. You know I was just sitting home waiting for calls and they never showed up. That’s how I started playing live again.
Oh that’s so interesting to me.

Well I figured the life of a musician comes in phases. It started with the big bands for me. I thought when the band broke up that was the end of the world. It wasn’t. I went on staff, I did the “Kate Smith Show.” While I was on the “Kate Smith Show” I subbed for the guitar player on the Three Suns, Morty (sic) [Al] Nevins, and I took his place. I put his tux on and I appeared as him. And I ended up playing with them for two years. I went to Vegas the first six weeks we were married we were in Vegas and we played from midnight to five in the morning.
